entry.evidence: although several tectonic faults are clearly documented in the geological map (Fig. 2), their potential Quaternary activity remains unknown

sequences.source_document: Published paper (XML full text, PDF for figures)

steps.action: Pose the problem that mapped faults around Ulaanbaatar have unknown Quaternary activity in a region of low recorded seismicity and growing exposure.
steps.quote: although several tectonic faults are clearly documented in the geological map (Fig. 2), their potential Quaternary activity remains unknown

steps.action: Cite the first author's thesis, in which satellite images and fieldwork led to the discovery of the Sharkhai and Avdar active faults south of the city.
steps.quote: we combined the analysis of high-resolution satellite images and field investigations and discovered two active faults hereafter called

steps.action: Map the fault trace on Pleiades HR images and SRTM/TanDEM-X DEMs: about 40 km long, strike N42 to N72, with a 1.4 km extensional jog that suggests two sections.
steps.quote: the main trace of the Sharkhai fault, striking ENE–WSW, extends along 40 km

steps.action: Check the remotely mapped trace in field campaigns that verify, correct and complement the image observations.
steps.quote: the surface trace can be followed on HR images and confirmed by field observations

steps.action: Estimate six cumulative left-lateral drainage offsets on the southern section (6.25 to 53 m) by back-slip reconstruction on images and DGPS topography, with combined measurement and resolution uncertainties.
steps.quote: we identified six cumulative left-lateral offsets

steps.action: Propose that the clustered 30 to 36 m offsets share a common climatic origin and age (a Late Pleistocene humid period); the hypothesis is not tested.
steps.quote: suggests the offset features may have a common climatic origin and thus age

steps.action: Measure the single northern-section offset (P7, 94 ± 3 m) and note that the fault tips under Quaternary plains may make the length an underestimate.
steps.quote: we measured 94 ± 3 m of left-lateral horizontal offset affecting a stream

steps.action: Take segmentation criteria from the literature: kilometre-scale discontinuities, and possibly strike changes above 5°, act as rupture barriers.
steps.quote: Usually, only kilometer-scale discontinuities are considered for the segmentation

steps.action: Compare the Sharkhai discontinuities with these criteria, using the Mogod and Bogd earthquakes as precedent, and keep only the central step-over as a possible segment boundary.
steps.quote: the changes in the orientation are either very local or not exceeding 9

steps.action: State two rival rupture scenarios: the whole 40 km fault breaks in one event, or the two 22 km segments break independently.
steps.quote: we propose two possible scenarios for large earthquakes on the Sharkhai fault

steps.action: Design the trench siting strategy: avoid wide alluvial valleys and target slow colluvial deposition and intermittent drainages, given an a priori slow deformation rate; select the Muka site.
steps.quote: our strategy was to avoid apparently recent deposits found in wide alluvial valleys

steps.action: Excavate two trenches across the 30 cm scarp; Muka-K collapsed after rain and permafrost thaw, so only Muka-L is analysed.
steps.quote: We excavated two trenches called Muka-K and Muka-L

steps.action: Clean, grid, photograph (210-photo mosaic) and log the trench walls, and describe units U70 to U10 with their depositional environments.
steps.quote: Both trench walls were cleaned, gridded, photographed and logged in detail.

steps.action: Compare the paleoseismic information on the east and west walls; they agree, so only the west wall is presented in detail.
steps.quote: Since both walls yield similar information in terms of paleoseismicity, we only present the west wall in detail

steps.action: Date five bulk-sediment samples by AMS radiocarbon, calibrated with OxCal and IntCal13, and discard W2-S05 as contaminated by rootlets and too young for its stratigraphic position.
steps.quote: we interpret W2-S05 as contaminated and rejuvenated with respect to its stratigraphic position and discard it from our analysis

steps.action: Exclude the bedrock (U70) shear zones as a record of recent events, because they are inconsistent with the ruptures in the overlying units.
steps.quote: it is therefore considered representative of an ancient tectonic regime

steps.action: Infer strike-slip, transtensional kinematics from flower structures, thickness changes, grabens and allochthonous blocks in the sedimentary section.
steps.quote: Splays with geometries resembling flower and double flower structures

steps.action: Use rupture terminations and abutting relationships to identify two event horizons: the penultimate event after U30 and before its erosion, and the most recent event after 775 CE; isolated ruptures are assigned to the most recent event rather than to a third event.
steps.quote: Abutting relationships reveal at least two deformation events.

steps.action: Bound the most recent event at 1778 CE because Ulaanbaatar's historical record, which begins then, reports no large earthquake on this fault.
steps.quote: a large earthquake after this date along this fault would have been reported in the historical documentation, which is not the case

steps.action: Derive the inter-event time from the two event windows: 2496 ± 887 years (1610 to 3383 years).
steps.quote: which yields an inter-event time of 2496 ± 887 years

steps.action: Compare the inter-event time with published values for major active faults elsewhere in Mongolia.
steps.quote: it is comparable to values derived for major active faults elsewhere in Mongolia

steps.action: Compute the magnitude and average co-seismic slip expected under each rupture scenario from rupture-length scaling regressions, since no single co-seismic offset was observed.
steps.quote: to associate magnitudes and co-seismic slip values to each scenario based on the length of the activated segments

steps.action: Run the scenario computation with two independent scaling relations (Wells and Coppersmith 1994; Leonard 2014) and tabulate both sets of results.
steps.quote: Estimation of the magnitude and average co-seismic slip using Wells and Coppersmith (1994) and Leonard (2014) regressions

steps.action: Estimate slip rates per scenario by dividing the scaled co-seismic slip by the inter-event time range: 0.2 to 0.8 mm/yr.
steps.quote: the slip rate would be between 0.4 ± 0.3 and 0.8 ± 0.6

steps.action: Check the timing, inter-event time and slip rates against the weak fault morphology, and judge the upper slip-rate bound unrealistic for a single structure.
steps.quote: appears unrealistically high for a single structure concerning region-wide values

steps.action: Compare with the local GPS network (3 ± 1 mm/yr ESE) and with published slip rates and recurrence times of the great western Mongolian faults (Table 5).
steps.quote: are about 2 to 10 times faster than those we estimate for the Sharkhai fault

steps.action: Keep the Sharkhai fault as a new hazard source with first estimates of magnitude, inter-event time and slip rate; both rupture scenarios are retained because the data do not favour either.
steps.quote: We suggest considering both scenarios, with the entire fault breaking in one event and the two segments breaking independently.

tree.answer: Yes: an active left-lateral fault with offset drainages and a subtle scarp
Partly: trace, offsets and trench ruptures are observed; ages, magnitudes and slip rates are inferred
Characterize geometry, kinematics and paleoseismicity of the fault for hazard assessment
Two rupture scenarios (whole fault vs two segments); in the trench, an intermediate event vs the most recent event
The scenarios predict different Mw and slip rates, but no data discriminate between them
Conditions found: trench site chosen; past events known only from traces

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: Two events in one trench and seven offset drainages; no second trench was analysed
Limited checks: field confirmation of the trace, agreement of both trench walls, two scaling laws
Estimates kept with wide uncertainties; rupture scenario left undecided
Reviewers are acknowledged, but no review file was supplied

end.claim: The Sharkhai fault is a ~40 km left-lateral active fault that produced two surface-rupturing earthquakes in the last ~3000 years (MRE 775-1778 CE; PE 1605-775/835 BCE), giving an inter-event time of 2496 ± 887 years and likely Mw 6.7 ± 0.2 or 7.1 ± 0.7 depending on segmentation.

decisive_move.sentence: Without dating the two event horizons in the Muka-L trench from abutting relationships and radiocarbon ages, there would be no evidence of Holocene surface faulting and no inter-event time, the paper's headline constraint.

gates.evidence: The working assumption that the fault is active and slow (from the inherited discovery) directed trench siting (§4 ¶1: 'Considering an a priori slow rate of deformation'). The trench could have shown no young ruptures, so fault activity faced a test it could have failed. The rupture scenarios were never tested against each other (§5.2 ¶7), and the magnitudes are regression outputs, not tests. Nothing was fixed before the data were seen.

imports.item: AMS radiocarbon dating of bulk sediment (Poznan Radiocarbon Laboratory)
OxCal calibration with the IntCal13 curve
Founding date of Ulaanbaatar (1778) and absence of a reported earthquake in historical documentation, used to bound the MRE
Pleiades 0.5 m panchromatic and 2 m multispectral imagery; TanDEM-X 12 m DEM

novelty_claims.quote: We present first constraints from tectonic geomorphology and paleoseismology along the newly discovered Sharkhai fault
The resulting time interval of 2496 ± 887 years is the first constraint for the Sharkhai fault for large earthquakes.
that was not characterized as active in previous studies
we conducted the first paleoseismological study along the Sharkhai Fault
[...] the first estimates on this fault of magnitude of a large event

limits: 1. The fault discovery is inherited from the first author's 2015 thesis; how and why it was first noticed is not shown here. 2. The paleoseismic record rests on one trench (Muka-L). The second trench (Muka-K) collapsed, and the site lies near the end of the mapped rupture, which the authors call non-standard; no independent trench or site replicates the two events. 3. Sub-claims at other statuses: (a) the rupture-scenario magnitudes (6.7 ± 0.2, 7.1 ± 0.7) and co-seismic slips are scaling-law expectations, not observations (no co-seismic offset was observed, §5.2 ¶2), and no scenario is favoured (§5.2 ¶7); (b) slip rates (0.2-0.8 mm/yr) are preliminary estimates; (c) the common climatic origin of the 30-36 m offsets is an untested hypothesis, and no offset is dated. 4. Internal inconsistencies in the text: the PE lower bound is given as 835 BCE (§0 ¶1, §4.2 ¶4) and as 775 BCE (§4.2 ¶5, §5.1 ¶3); the inter-event time is 2496 ± 887 yr but 2496 ± 88 yr in §5.3 ¶2; segment lengths are 22 km (§3 ¶3) and 20 km (§5.2 ¶1); the central jog is called a right step (§2.1.2 ¶1) and a left step-over (Figure 3, Figure 5). 5. The 1778 CE upper bound depends on the inference that the historical record is complete for this fault; the authors assume this without discussion. 6. OSL dating is mentioned as a possibility (§4 ¶1), but only radiocarbon is reported; inference: OSL was not done or not reported. 7. The coded checks are thin (field confirmation, two walls, two regressions); no sensitivity of the event chronology to sample selection is reported.

disagreements.target: Geologic map of Mongolia (Tomurtogoo et al., 1998)
disagreements.support: Offset drainages, scarps and trench ruptures show that a mapped geological structure, not previously characterized as active, is an active fault.
disagreements.quote: the surface rupture corresponds to a documented geological structure (Fig. 2) that was not characterized as active in previous studies

disagreements.target: Proposal that strike changes of more than 5° act as segment boundaries (Lettis et al., 2002; Harris et al., 1991; [...]
disagreements.support: The 1967 Mogod and 1957 Bogd Mongolian ruptures crossed larger bends, so the authors do not treat the Sharkhai strike changes (≤9°) as boundaries.
disagreements.quote: Nevertheless, recent large earthquakes in Mongolia have shown that even larger changes in orientation had no impact on the fault segmentation

alternatives_considered.chosen: Only the 1.4 km central step-over as a potential segment boundary
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Small step-overs (3-173 m) and strike changes above 5° as segment boundaries
alternatives_considered.reason: Literature considers only kilometre-scale discontinuities; Mongolian ruptures crossed larger bends

alternatives_considered.chosen: Both Wells and Coppersmith (1994) and Leonard (2014) regressions
alternatives_considered.reason: Leonard (2014) described as more recent work

alternatives_considered.chosen: Colluvium on gentle slopes and intermittent drainages (Muka site)
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Recent deposits in wide alluvial valleys
alternatives_considered.reason: Alluvial deposits could cover recent deformation or erode the last event records

alternatives_considered.chosen: Trench site near the end of the mapped rupture
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Standard strategy of trenching away from the rupture end
alternatives_considered.reason: Potential sites are scarce; this site has relatively high sedimentary potential

alternatives_considered.reason: Sits close to a rupture with dense live rootlets; interpreted as contaminated and rejuvenated

alternatives_considered.reason: Their upward continuation could not be observed because U11 lacks clear stratigraphy
